unit.subtitle: Beliefs and practices of Islam as the second religion

lessons.title: Core Muslim Beliefs and the Nature of Allah
lessons.description: Tawhid, the Six Beliefs, the Five Roots of Shi'a Islam, Risalah and the holy books.
lessons.content_html:
Tawhid: The Oneness of Allah

The single most fundamental belief in Islam is Tawhid (Arabic: ‘oneness’). Allah is one, indivisible, eternal and without any partner, associate or equal. Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas — ‘Sincerity’) states: “Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor was born, nor is there any equivalent to Him.” Surah 112 is the most-recited summary of Tawhid and is used to correct any association of partners with Allah (shirk), which is considered the gravest sin in Islam.

The characteristics of Allah described in the Qur’an include: oneness (Tawhid), immanence (closeness to creation), transcendence (beyond creation), omnipotence (all-powerful), beneficence and mercy (Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim), fairness and justice. Surah 16:35–36 emphasises that Allah sent messengers to every community to call them to worship him alone.

In Shi’a Islam, divine justice has a special name: Adalat. It is listed as one of the Five Roots and underscores that God’s justice is perfect — he does not oppress, and human beings genuinely have free will because a just God must leave room for real moral choice.

Key Fact

Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) is the Qur’anic anchor for Tawhid: Allah is “the One, the Eternal Refuge” who “neither begets nor was born.” Shirk (associating partners with Allah) is the greatest sin in Islam because it violates Tawhid directly.

The Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam

Sunni Islam organises its core beliefs into six beliefs, drawn from Kitab al-iman 1:4 (a hadith of the Prophet). They are:

  1. Belief in Allah (Tawhid — the oneness of God)
  2. Belief in his Angels (Malaikah) — pure, obedient spiritual beings
  3. Belief in his Holy Books (Kutub) — revelations sent to the prophets
  4. Belief in his Prophets (Risalah) — messengers from Adam to Muhammad
  5. Belief in the Day of Judgement (Akhirah) — the final reckoning and afterlife
  6. Belief in divine decree (al-Qadr) — Allah’s knowledge of and sovereignty over all events

Shi’a Islam uses a different organising structure: the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din:

  • Tawhid — the oneness of Allah (Surah 112)
  • ‘Adl (divine justice/Adalat) — Allah always acts justly; human beings have real moral freedom
  • Nubuwwah — prophethood; Allah communicated through a line of prophets ending with Muhammad
  • Imamah — the leadership of the Imams, direct successors to Muhammad from the Prophet’s family (Ahl al-Bayt); this is distinctive to Shi’a Islam
  • Mi’ad — the Day of Resurrection and Judgement

Critical distinction: The Five Roots are Shi’a. The Six Beliefs are Sunni. Do not conflate them in exam answers.

Risalah: Prophethood

Risalah is the belief in prophethood: that Allah chose specific human beings to receive and convey his guidance to the world. Surah 2:136 names the key prophets believed in by Muslims: “We believe in Allah, and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses, Jesus and the Prophets from their Lord.”

The named prophets in this spec are: Adam (the first human being and first prophet), Ibrahim (Abraham — friend of God, father of monotheism), Musa (Moses — who received the Tawrat/Torah), Isa (Jesus — regarded as a great prophet and the Messiah, born of the virgin Maryam, but not the Son of God) and Muhammad (the final and greatest prophet, ‘seal of the Prophets’).

The Holy Books (Kutub)

Muslims believe Allah revealed holy books to his prophets. The Kutub (holy books) include: the Qur’an (revealed to Muhammad, in Arabic, the final and uncorrupted revelation), the Tawrat (Torah, revealed to Musa/Moses), the Zabur (Psalms, revealed to Dawud/David), and the Injil (Gospel, revealed to Isa/Jesus). Muslims believe the earlier books became corrupted over time — the Qur’an alone remains in its original form and therefore has supreme authority.

Both Islam and Christianity affirm that God is one, all-powerful, all-knowing, and merciful. However, there are significant differences:

  • Tawhid vs Trinity: Islam emphatically rejects the Christian Trinity as shirk (associating partners with God). Surah 112 directly refutes any idea that God has offspring or equals. Christians argue that the Trinity is a refined understanding of monotheism — one God in three Persons — not polytheism, but Muslims regard this distinction as insufficient.
  • Prophethood of Isa: Islam affirms Jesus (Isa) as a great prophet, born of the Virgin Maryam, the Messiah, and a worker of miracles — but emphatically not the Son of God or divine. The Christian claim that Jesus is God incarnate is rejected in Islamic theology as a violation of Tawhid.
  • Personal relationship: Both traditions affirm that God/Allah is close to his creation. The Qur’an teaches that Allah is “closer to him [the human] than his jugular vein” (Surah 50:16). Christians express this through the Incarnation — God entering human experience directly in Jesus.
Key Fact

Muslims believe earlier books (Tawrat, Zabur, Injil) were gradually corrupted by human error or alteration. The Qur’an, revealed to Muhammad in Arabic and preserved in its original form, is the final, uncorrupted Word of Allah. This is why the Qur’an has supreme authority in Islam.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A very common error: writing that the Six Beliefs and Five Roots are the same thing. They are not — the Six Beliefs are Sunni; the Five Roots are Shi’a. The key difference is Imamah (Shi’a) and al-Qadr (Sunni). The 5-mark Explain question on Tawhid or Risalah will require a named source: use Surah 112 for Tawhid, or Surah 2:136 for Risalah/prophethood — both are in your spec and are safe citations. Do NOT invent Qur’an references. For the 12-mark Discuss: “Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam.” Develop for (Tawhid is the first and most fundamental belief; shirk is the greatest sin; it organises all other Islamic doctrine) and against (Risalah is equally essential — without prophets Muslims would have no Qur’an or guidance; the Day of Judgement may be more personally motivating). Correctly spell technical terms: ‘Tawhid’, ‘Risalah’, ‘shirk’, ‘Kutub’ — SPaG marks reward precision.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Tawhid (the absolute oneness of Allah) is the foundation of all Islamic belief; Surah 112 is its Qur’anic anchor; shirk (associating partners) is the greatest sin.
  • Sunni Islam has Six Beliefs; Shi’a Islam has the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din — the unique Shi’a addition is Imamah (the leadership of the Imams). Do not conflate them.
  • Risalah (prophethood) is expressed in Surah 2:136; key prophets include Adam, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad. Muslims accept all four holy books but regard the Qur’an as the final, uncorrupted revelation.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Muslim beliefs about the holy books (Kutub).

practice_questions.text: 'Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam.' Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. FOR: Tawhid is the first and foundational belief; shirk (violation of Tawhid) is the only unforgivable sin in Islamic theology; Surah 112 reduces all of Islam to this single truth; every Islamic practice (Salah, Shahada, Hajj) expresses Tawhid. AGAINST: Risalah is equally essential — without prophets and the Qur'an, no Muslim would know how to worship Allah; the Day of Judgement may be more practically motivating for daily Islamic life; Shi'a Muslims might argue Imamah is distinctively important for their community. Named sources: Surah 112; Surah 2:136; Surah 16:35–36. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

glossary_terms.definition: The Islamic doctrine of the absolute oneness, uniqueness and indivisibility of Allah — the foundational belief that no associate, partner or equal exists alongside God.

The Shi'a Islamic principle of divine justice, holding that Allah always acts justly and that human beings have real moral freedom because Allah would not hold them responsible for actions they could not freely choose.
The six fundamental beliefs of Sunni Islam: belief in Allah, his angels, his holy books, his prophets, the Day of Judgement, and divine decree (al-Qadr).
The five foundational principles of Shi'a Islam: Tawhid (oneness), Adl (justice), Nubuwwah (prophethood), Imamah (leadership), and Mi'ad (resurrection).
The Islamic belief in prophethood — that Allah communicated his will to humanity through a succession of prophets, beginning with Adam and ending with Muhammad as the 'seal of the Prophets.'
The Muslim collective term for the holy books revealed by Allah, including the Qur'an, the Tawrat, the Zabur and the Injil.

lessons.title: Angels, Predestination and Akhirah
lessons.description: Malaikah, al-Qadr and Muslim teaching on life after death — plus comparison with Christian afterlife.
lessons.content_html:
Malaikah: Angels in Islam

Malaikah (singular: malak) are angels — spiritual beings created by Allah from light (nur). They have no free will; they exist only to obey Allah. They are not depicted with wings or human form in Islamic theology, though the Qur’an uses figurative language. Angels are part of the unseen world (al-ghayb).

Three angels are particularly significant in Islamic belief:

  • Jibril (Gabriel): the angel of revelation, through whom Allah communicated the Qur’an to Muhammad. Surah 2:97–98 states: “Whoever is an enemy of Jibril — it is he who has brought the Qur’an down upon your heart.” Jibril also appeared to Maryam to announce the birth of Isa.
  • Mika’il (Michael): the angel of sustenance and mercy, associated with rain, provision and natural phenomena that sustain life. Surah 2:98 mentions him alongside Jibril.
  • Izra’il: the angel of death, who takes the soul at the moment of death. Surah 32:11 states: “The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take you, and then you will be returned to your Lord.” Izra’il serves as a reminder that death is controlled by Allah, not by chance.

The Qur’an also names Kiraman Katibin — the two recording angels assigned to every person, noting their deeds. These records will be opened on the Day of Judgement.

Key Fact

Three named angels: Jibril (revelation, Surah 2:97–98), Mika’il (sustenance, Surah 2:98), Izra’il (death, Surah 32:11). All are created from light, have no free will, and carry out Allah’s commands perfectly.

Al-Qadr: Predestination

Al-Qadr is the Arabic term for divine decree or predestination. Muslims believe that Allah has complete foreknowledge of all events and that nothing falls outside his will. The hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 relates the Prophet Muhammad’s teaching that every human being is created with their fate ‘written’ by an angel before birth, including their provision, lifespan, deeds and whether they will enter paradise or the fire.

This doctrine is one of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam. It teaches that human beings are not independent agents operating outside Allah’s knowledge, but it does not eliminate human moral responsibility: Muslims are still judged on the basis of their choices.

Sunni and Shi’a approaches to predestination differ in emphasis:

  • Sunni Islam holds that al-Qadr is one of the Six Beliefs: Allah knows and decrees all things. Most Sunni theologians teach that both divine foreknowledge and genuine human free will coexist, though how this is possible is a theological mystery (taqdeer). Human beings choose and are accountable; Allah knows those choices in advance.
  • Shi’a Islam places greater emphasis on Adl (divine justice) as the governing principle. A just God would not predetermine a person’s actions and then punish them — therefore, humans must have genuine freedom. Shi’a theology generally stresses human free will more strongly than some Sunni accounts.

Akhirah: Life After Death

Akhirah means ‘the hereafter’ or ‘the afterlife.’ It encompasses the events that follow death: the intermediate state (barzakh), the resurrection, the Day of Judgement, and the final destinations of paradise (Jannah) or hell (Jahannam).

Surah 17:49–72 is a key Qur’anic passage on Akhirah. It describes sceptics asking how God could resurrect decomposed bones, to which the answer is: “Say: Be you stones or iron, or [any] creation of that which is great within your breasts. And they will say, ‘Who will restore us?’ Say, ‘He who created you the first time.’” Allah, who created from nothing, can certainly resurrect the dead.

The sequence of events in Islamic eschatology:

  1. Death and Barzakh: After death the soul enters a waiting state (barzakh — the ‘barrier’ between this world and the Day of Judgement).
  2. Resurrection: On the Last Day, all souls are resurrected bodily.
  3. Judgement: Each person’s deeds are weighed on scales (mizan). The recording angels’ books are opened. Allah’s mercy also plays a decisive role — he may forgive those whose deeds are insufficient.
  4. Jannah or Jahannam: The righteous enter Jannah (paradise) — a garden of eternal bliss in the presence of Allah. The unrighteous enter Jahannam (hell) — a place of fire and separation from God.

The comparison below highlights key differences between Islamic and Christian afterlife beliefs:

  • Both traditions teach bodily resurrection, final judgement, paradise and a place of punishment. Both hold that earthly life shapes eternal destiny.
  • Islam: no purgatory or intermediate purification state (other than barzakh as a waiting state). Judgement is based on the weighing of deeds. The role of a mediating figure (like Christ in Christianity) is absent — Allah alone judges, though his mercy is decisive.
  • Christianity (Catholic): purgatory allows purification after death for those not fully ready for heaven. Salvation is achieved through faith in Christ, whose atoning death ‘pays’ for sin — a concept absent from Islam. Protestant Christianity rejects purgatory.
  • Key difference: Islamic judgement is more explicitly deed-based with direct divine mercy; Catholic Christianity builds in an intermediate purification stage and grounds salvation in Christ’s atonement.
Key Fact

Islamic eschatology sequence: death → barzakh (waiting state) → resurrection → judgement (deeds weighed on mizan) → Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell). Surah 17:49–72 is the key Qur’anic passage on resurrection.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The 2C 1.8* marker means a 12-mark Discuss question comparing Muslim and Christian afterlife is very likely: “Islam and Christianity have the same beliefs about life after death.” The sharpest contrast is purgatory (Catholic Christianity) vs no purgatory (Islam); and atonement through Christ (Christianity) vs deed-based judgement with divine mercy (Islam). Develop both sides with named sources: Surah 17:49–72 for Islamic resurrection; 2 Corinthians 5:1–10 or the 39 Articles for Christian afterlife. For the 5-mark Explain on predestination, Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 is the spec-named hadith — cite it as ‘Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685’ to earn the source mark. Do not write ‘a hadith says...’ without naming the collection. Correct spelling of ‘Akhirah’, ‘Malaikah’, ‘al-Qadr’ earns SPaG marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Malaikah (angels) are created from light, without free will: Jibril brings revelation (Surah 2:97–98), Mika’il oversees sustenance, and Izra’il takes souls at death (Surah 32:11).
  • Al-Qadr (divine decree) is one of the Sunni Six Beliefs; Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 is the hadith anchor; Shi’a Islam stresses Adl (justice) and human free will more strongly than some Sunni accounts.
  • Akhirah includes death, barzakh, resurrection, judgement (mizan) and Jannah or Jahannam; Surah 17:49–72 is the key passage; the key contrast with Christian afterlife is the absence of purgatory and the deed-based (not atonement-based) judgement in Islam.

Three separately identifiable roles.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about life after death (Akhirah).
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) Bodily resurrection — on the Last Day Allah will raise all the dead, regardless of what has happened to the body; Surah 17 responds to sceptics asking how God can raise decomposed bones; (2) Judgement — each person's deeds are weighed on scales (mizan) and the recording angels' books are opened; Allah's mercy also plays a decisive role. Development beyond bare statements required.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about Malaikah, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Jibril is the angel of revelation — Surah 2:97–98 states he brought the Qur'an down upon the heart of Muhammad; without Jibril Muslims would have no Qur'an; (2) Izra'il is the angel of death — Surah 32:11 describes him as 'entrusted with you', taking the soul at the appointed time. 5th mark requires a named source: Surah 2:97–98 or Surah 32:11.

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between Muslim and Catholic Christian beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete contrasts: (1) Islam has no purgatory; Catholicism teaches purgatory as a state of purification after death; (2) In Islam, judgement is based on deeds weighed on scales (mizan) with divine mercy; in Christianity, salvation comes through faith in Christ's atoning sacrifice; (3) Islam emphasises barzakh (waiting state between death and judgement); most Christian denominations have no equivalent concept.

practice_questions.text: 'Muslim and Christian beliefs about life after death are more similar than different.' Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. FOR: both teach bodily resurrection, final judgement, and eternal destinations (Jannah/heaven, Jahannam/hell); both hold that earthly life shapes eternal destiny; both see God/Allah as just and merciful in judgement. AGAINST: purgatory (Catholic Christianity) is absent from Islam; Christianity grounds salvation in Christ's atonement — a concept absent from Islamic theology; the role of the Imam in Shi'a Islam has no Christian equivalent; Protestant Christianity (39 Articles) and Islamic teaching both reject purgatory but for different reasons. Named sources: Surah 17:49–72; 2 Corinthians 5:1–10; 39 Articles. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

lessons.title: The Five Pillars and Ten Obligatory Acts
lessons.description: Shahadah, Salah, Sawm, Zakah and Hajj; the Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi'a Islam; Khums.
lessons.content_html:
The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

Islam is built on five core practices known as the Five Pillars. These are not optional extras — they are fard (compulsory) for every adult Muslim of sound mind. Together they shape a Muslim’s daily life, social relationships and relationship with Allah. The Prophet Muhammad described Islam as being “built upon five things” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari). Surah 3:17–21 praises those who are patient, truthful, devout, and charitable — qualities embodied by the Five Pillars.

Key Fact

The Five Pillars: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakah (2.5% of savings given to those in need), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah at least once). This is the foundational framework of Sunni practice.

Shahadah — Declaration of Faith

The Shahadah is the declaration: “There is no God but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah.” It is the most fundamental act of Islamic faith. Reciting it sincerely and with understanding is the act that makes a person Muslim. It is whispered in a newborn’s ear, said at regular intervals in prayer and at the hour of death. Surah 3:17–21 describes those who consistently bear witness (“shahada”) to Allah’s oneness as among the most praiseworthy of believers.

Salah — Prayer

Salah is compulsory prayer five times a day: Fajr (before sunrise), Zuhr (after midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (after sunset) and Isha (night). Before praying, Muslims perform wudu (ritual washing). On Fridays, Sunni Muslim men are expected to pray Jummah (the Friday congregational prayer) at the mosque. Surah 29:45 states: “Recite what has been revealed to you of the Scripture; keep up the prayer — prayer restrains outrageous and unacceptable behaviour.” Surah 15:98–99 connects glorification of Allah in prayer with certainty of faith. Shi’a Muslims perform the same five prayers but may combine them into three prayer times during the day.

Sawm — Fasting

Sawm involves complete fasting during the holy month of Ramadan. Muslims abstain from all food, drink, smoking and sexual relations from dawn to sunset. Surah 2:183–185 commands: “You who believe, fasting is prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may be mindful of God.” Within Ramadan, the Laylat al-Qadr (Night of Power) commemorates the first revelation of the Qur’an to Muhammad and is described in the Qur’an as better than a thousand months of worship. Those who cannot fast (due to illness, pregnancy or travel) may break their fast and compensate later. Ramadan ends with the festival of Id-ul-Fitr.

Zakah — Almsgiving

Zakah means “purification” or “growth.” It requires every Muslim whose savings exceed the nisab (minimum threshold) to give 2.5% of their annual savings to those in need. Surah 9:58–60 specifies eight categories of those entitled to receive Zakah, including the poor, the indebted and travellers in need. Zakah purifies the giver’s remaining wealth from greed, supports the poor and reduces inequality within the ummah (global Muslim community).

Hajj — Pilgrimage

Hajj takes place in the twelfth month of the Islamic calendar and must be performed at least once in a lifetime by every Muslim who is physically and financially able. Surah 2:124–130 describes Ibrahim and Isma’il building the Ka’aba and establishing the rites of pilgrimage. Surah 22:25–30 describes the sacred sites and the command to proclaim Hajj to all people. Hajj rites include walking around the Ka’aba seven times (tawaf), walking between the hills of Safa and Marwa, standing on the plain of Arafat (wuquf), and symbolically stoning the devil. Hajj creates a profound sense of equality and unity — all pilgrims wear identical white garments (ihram), erasing distinctions of wealth and rank.

  • Islam: Salah is compulsory five times daily; all pray in Arabic using set movements; facing Makkah (qibla); preceded by wudu. Jummah (Friday prayer) is a communal obligation for men.
  • Catholic Christianity: The Mass is the central act of worship — the Eucharist (the source and summit of Catholic life, Lumen Gentium 7). Catholics attend Sunday Mass as an obligation. Prayer takes many forms: formal (the Divine Office) and informal. No single fixed time structure equivalent to the five daily prayers.
  • General Christianity: Worship varies widely — liturgical (set structure, e.g. Anglican) and non-liturgical (free-form, e.g. Baptist). Prayer is encouraged but not prescribed at fixed times in the way Islamic Salah is.

The Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims have their own framework of obligatory acts. While the Five Pillars are broadly shared, Shi’a Islam lists Ten Obligatory Acts (Furu ad-Din — branches of religion). These include Salah, Sawm, Zakah and Hajj (shared with Sunni Islam), but add several distinctively Shi’a duties: Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income), Jihad (striving in the way of Allah), Amr-bil-Maroof (commanding what is right), and Nahy-anil-Munkar (forbidding what is wrong). Khums is particularly significant: Surah 8:41 specifies that a fifth of certain gains should be set aside “for Allah and the Messenger,” which Shi’a Muslims understand as a continuing obligation paid to the Imam’s representatives (the religious scholars).

Key Fact

Khums (20% of surplus income) is a Shi’a-specific obligation distinct from Sunni Zakah (2.5% of savings above nisab). Khums is paid to the Imam’s representatives (religious scholars) for religious and charitable purposes. Both Zakah and Khums serve to reduce inequality within the ummah, but they operate on different rates and through different channels.

The Five Pillars are the universal Sunni framework of practice. The Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam (Wajibat) include the Five Pillars (Salah, Sawm, Zakah, Hajj, and Shahadah through Walayah) plus additional obligations: Khums (20% levy), Jihad, commanding good, forbidding evil, and love/disavowal (Tawallah and Tabarra). Some scholars count the Ten differently, but Khums is the distinctive Shi’a addition. The underlying logic is the same: both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims structure their lives around prescribed acts of worship that express submission to Allah.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 5-mark “Explain two… with sources” questions on Islamic practice, use these named anchors: Salah — Surah 29:45 or Surah 15:98–99; Sawm — Surah 2:183–185; Zakah — Surah 9:58–60; Hajj — Surah 2:124–130 or Surah 22:25–30. For the 12-mark Discuss on worship (2.3*), develop both Islamic and another tradition’s practice with equal depth — the Sunni–Shi’a difference on Salah (three times vs five) and on obligatory acts (Five Pillars vs Ten Obligatory Acts including Khums) is a rich source of developed contrast. The most common failure is a Discuss answer that treats “another point of view” as a single brief sentence. SPaG: spell Shahadah, Zakah, Ramadan and Khums correctly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam are Shahadah, Salah, Zakah (2.5% of savings), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan, commanded in Surah 2:183–185) and Hajj to Makkah (anchored in Surah 2:124–130 and Surah 22:25–30).
  • Shi’a Islam has Ten Obligatory Acts (Furu ad-Din), adding Khums (20% of surplus income), Jihad, and duties to command good and forbid evil — making Khums a key Sunni–Shi’a difference in practice.
  • Salah (2.3*) is a starred spec point: Sunni Muslims pray five times daily; Shi’a may combine into three times. Hajj creates equality through ihram. The Friday congregational prayer (Jummah) is obligatory for adult Sunni Muslim men.

practice_questions.text: Outline three of the Five Pillars of Sunni Islam.
practice_questions.model_answer: Three from: Shahadah (declaration of faith: 'There is no God but Allah and Muhammad is His messenger'); Salah (five daily prayers); Zakah (giving 2.5% of annual savings to those in need); Sawm (fasting during Ramadan); Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah at least once in a lifetime). One mark per clearly distinct pillar with its English meaning.

practice_questions.text: Describe the significance of Hajj for Muslims.
practice_questions.model_answer: Hajj is the fifth pillar of Islam and compulsory at least once for Muslims who are able. It takes place in Makkah, the holiest city in Islam. Pilgrims wear identical white garments (ihram), symbolising equality before Allah. Hajj commemorates the actions of Ibrahim and Isma'il. It unites Muslims globally and spiritually renews the individual. Three descriptive points earn three marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Sunni and Shi'a obligations in Islamic practice.
practice_questions.model_answer: First difference: Sunni Islam has the Five Pillars; Shi'a Islam has Ten Obligatory Acts (Furu ad-Din). The Shi'a framework adds Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income), Jihad as an obligation, and duties to command good and forbid wrong. This reflects Shi'a theology's emphasis on active social justice and the role of the Imam's representatives. Second difference: The Zakah rate differs. Sunni Zakah is 2.5% of savings above the nisab. Shi'a Khums is 20% of surplus income, paid to religious scholars acting as representatives of the Imam. This difference in rate and recipient reflects the distinct Shi'a belief in Imamah and the ongoing role of religious leadership. Two developed points, two marks each.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Salah is important for Muslims.
In your answer you must refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.model_answer: First reason: Salah structures a Muslim's day around remembrance of Allah. By praying five times daily, a Muslim is reminded of Allah's presence throughout every activity. Surah 29:45 states: 'Keep up the prayer — prayer restrains outrageous and unacceptable behaviour.' This shows that Salah is not merely ritual — it actively shapes moral conduct. Second reason: Salah unites the global ummah. Whether praying in London, Jakarta or Cairo, all Muslims face the qibla (Makkah), pray in Arabic and follow the same movements. This creates a profound sense of shared identity. The fifth mark requires Surah 29:45 as the named anchor.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the statement: 'The Five Pillars are all equally important for Muslims.'
In your answer you should give developed arguments in support of and against this statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.model_answer: Arguments in support: Each pillar addresses a different but essential dimension of Muslim faith and practice. Shahadah establishes identity; Salah maintains daily contact with God; Zakah expresses social responsibility; Sawm builds spiritual discipline; Hajj connects the believer to Islamic origins and the global ummah. Neglecting any one weakens the others — as the Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari suggests, Islam is built on all five. Together they form an integrated structure, not a hierarchy. Arguments against: The Shahadah is often described as the most fundamental, since it is the act of becoming Muslim and is embedded within every other pillar. Without affirming the oneness of Allah and the prophethood of Muhammad, the other four pillars are meaningless. Some scholars prioritise Salah as the pillar that is most regularly practised and that most consistently shapes Muslim identity. Hajj is the only pillar many Muslims never perform (due to financial or health constraints), and exemptions exist for Sawm — suggesting these are contextually flexible in ways Salah and Zakah are not. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might argue that the Shahadah is logically primary (it defines what it means to be Muslim) but that in terms of daily impact, Salah is the most shaping practice. The pillars are interdependent rather than strictly equal in weight — their importance varies by context and by individual circumstance. Mastering (10-12): both sides with named sources (Sahih al-Bukhari, Surah references); weighing explicit; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides; one source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant. Emerging (1-3): brief and one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of the Hajj pilgrimage.
practice_questions.model_answer: Three from: walking seven times around the Ka'aba (tawaf); walking between the hills of Safa and Marwa; standing on the plain of Arafat (wuquf); symbolically stoning the devil; wearing ihram (white garments symbolising equality); animal sacrifice commemorating Ibrahim's willingness; visiting the mosque in Makkah. One mark per clearly distinct feature.

glossary_terms.definition: The Islamic declaration of faith: 'There is no God but Allah, and Muhammad is His messenger.' Sincerely reciting this is the act of becoming Muslim.
Compulsory ritual prayer performed five times daily by Muslims, involving specific movements, recitations and conditions of purity.
Ritual washing (ablution) performed before prayer, involving washing the hands, face, arms, head and feet in a set order.
Obligatory almsgiving in Sunni Islam — 2.5% of annual savings above the nisab threshold given to those in need.
Fasting during the month of Ramadan — abstaining from food, drink, smoking and sexual relations from dawn to sunset.
The annual pilgrimage to Makkah, compulsory at least once in a lifetime for Muslims who are physically and financially able.
A Shi'a Islamic tax of 20% of annual surplus income, paid to religious scholars for charitable and religious purposes.
The Friday congregational prayer, compulsory for adult Muslim men, held at the mosque at midday on Fridays.
The Night of Power — one of the last ten nights of Ramadan, believed to mark the first revelation of the Qur'an to Muhammad.

lessons.title: Jihad and Islamic Festivals
lessons.description: Lesser and greater Jihad; Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, Id-ul-Ghadeer and Ashura.
lessons.content_html:
Jihad — Striving in the Way of Allah

The word jihad means “struggle” or “striving.” It does not mean “holy war” — that is a common mistranslation. Every Muslim is engaged in jihad whenever they strive to be a better person, resist temptation, act justly or work for a fairer society. Islam recognises two forms of jihad: greater jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) and lesser jihad (al-jihad al-asghar).

Key Fact

Greater jihad is the struggle against nafs (the lower self) — the daily effort to be honest, compassionate, self-disciplined and obedient to Allah. Classical scholars held that this inward struggle is the most difficult and most continuous form of jihad. Lesser jihad refers to defensive struggle to protect the Muslim community under conditions tightly constrained by Islamic jurisprudence.

Greater Jihad — The Inner Struggle

Greater jihad involves resisting the temptation to lie, be selfish, be unjust or neglect religious duties. It includes studying Islam, raising a family according to Islamic values, working honestly, caring for parents and being a good neighbour. Every act of worship — Salah, Sawm, Zakah — is itself a form of greater jihad, since each requires the believer to overcome laziness, selfishness or distraction to submit to Allah. Greater jihad is lifelong; it ends only at death.

Lesser Jihad — Conditions and Constraints

Lesser jihad refers to the use of force to defend the Muslim community, resist oppression or uphold justice. It is not a licence for aggression. Surah 2:190–194 sets clear conditions: “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress, for Allah does not love transgressors.” The passage prohibits fighting those who do not fight, prohibits attacking during sacred months and commands that fighting must stop when the enemy ceases hostilities. Surah 22:39 permits Muslims who have been wronged to fight in self-defence: “Permission to fight is given to those who have been attacked.”

Classical Islamic jurisprudence lists conditions that must be met before lesser jihad is permissible:

  • There must be a legitimate cause — typically self-defence or the defence of those being oppressed.
  • All peaceful alternatives must have been exhausted first.
  • It must be declared by a legitimate authority (not by individuals acting alone).
  • Non-combatants — women, children, the elderly, clergy and those not fighting — must be protected. Destruction of crops and buildings is prohibited.
  • It must cease when the enemy stops fighting or offers peace (Surah 2:192–193).

These conditions mean that lesser jihad is constrained in classical Islamic teaching far more than media portrayals often suggest. Extremist interpretations that remove these conditions are rejected by mainstream Islamic scholars.

Reducing jihad to “holy war” misrepresents Islamic teaching in two ways. First, it ignores greater jihad, which classical scholars considered the more important form. Second, it strips lesser jihad of its strict conditions — making it sound like permission for unlimited violence, which the Qur’an explicitly prohibits. Surah 2:190 states: “do not transgress, for Allah does not love transgressors.” Exam answers that describe jihad only as “holy war” will score poorly; both forms must be covered.

Islamic Festivals

Islamic festivals unite the global ummah in shared acts of worship, remembrance and celebration. Four key festivals feature in the specification: Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, Id-ul-Ghadeer (Shi’a) and Ashura.

Id-ul-Adha — Festival of Sacrifice

Id-ul-Adha (the Festival of Sacrifice) is one of the two major Islamic festivals. It commemorates Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son at Allah’s command. Surah 37:77–111 recounts the story: Ibrahim was commanded in a dream to sacrifice his son; he informed his son, who submitted willingly. As Ibrahim prepared to act, Allah intervened and provided a ram as a substitute, rewarding Ibrahim’s faith with the announcement that he had fulfilled the vision. Most Muslim scholars identify the son as Isma’il, though the Qur’an does not name him in this passage — the identification is traditional, not explicitly stated. Id-ul-Adha takes place during the Hajj period and involves the sacrifice of an animal (qurbani), with meat shared among family, friends and the poor.

Id-ul-Fitr — Festival Marking the End of Ramadan

Id-ul-Fitr celebrates the successful completion of the month-long Ramadan fast. It begins with a communal prayer and sermon at the mosque. Muslims give Zakat al-Fitr (a special obligatory charity at Ramadan’s end) so that everyone in the community can celebrate. The festival continues with visiting family, feasting, wearing new or clean clothes, and giving gifts to children. Id-ul-Fitr is a celebration of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete Sawm and a joyful acknowledgement of the community that fasted together.

Id-ul-Ghadeer — A Shi’a Festival

Id-ul-Ghadeer is one of the most important Shi’a festivals. It commemorates the event at Ghadir Khumm (on the return from the Prophet’s final Hajj in 632 CE) when, according to Shi’a belief, the Prophet Muhammad announced that Ali ibn Abi Talib was to be his rightful successor. Shi’a Muslims understand Surah 5:3 — “Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My blessing upon you” — as referring to this proclamation at Ghadir. Sunni Muslims interpret this verse differently, associating it with the completion of the Hajj rather than a specific designation of Ali. Id-ul-Ghadeer is therefore a specifically Shi’a festival with profound significance for the doctrine of Imamah.

Ashura — A Day of Contrasting Significance

Ashura falls on the tenth day of Muharram (the first month of the Islamic calendar) and holds very different significance for Sunni and Shi’a Muslims.

Sunni Ashura: For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is primarily a day of voluntary fasting. A hadith recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari reports that when the Prophet arrived in Madinah and observed the Jewish community fasting, he was told it was the day Moses was saved from Pharaoh. The Prophet reportedly said he had a stronger connection to Moses and encouraged fasting on this day. It is an act of gratitude rather than mourning.

Shi’a Ashura: For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year — a day of mourning and lamentation for the martyrdom of Imam Husayn (the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and the third Shi’a Imam) at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn and his small band were killed by the forces of Caliph Yazid after refusing to pledge allegiance to what Shi’a Muslims regard as an unjust ruler. Ashura is marked with processions, passionate re-enactments (ta’ziyeh), lamentations and the retelling of Husayn’s sacrifice. The tragedy of Karbala is central to Shi’a religious identity and theology.

Key Fact

Islamic festivals in this spec: Id-ul-Fitr (end of Ramadan — Sunni and Shi’a), Id-ul-Adha (feast of sacrifice, Ibrahim — Sunni and Shi’a), Ashura (Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala — primarily Shi’a), Id-ul-Ghadeer (Muhammad’s designation of Ali — Shi’a). Surah 37:77–111 is the Qur’anic account of Ibrahim’s sacrifice that Id-ul-Adha commemorates.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The jihad topic is flagged as the highest-risk misconception in the teaching brief. If asked to “outline three aspects of jihad,” you must cover: (1) the meaning of the word (“striving”), (2) greater jihad (inner struggle against nafs), (3) lesser jihad (outward, defensive, under strict conditions). Do not reduce it to “holy war.” For 5-mark “Explain two with sources,” use Surah 2:190–194 for lesser jihad and Surah 22:39 for the permission to defend. For Id-ul-Ghadeer, Surah 5:3 is the Edexcel anchor. For Ashura, name both Sunni (voluntary fast — Sahih al-Bukhari) and Shi’a (Karbala martyrdom) interpretations — examiners expect both. SPaG: spell Jihad, Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Ghadeer and Ashura correctly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jihad means striving: greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle against the lower self) is the continuous, primary form; lesser jihad (outward defence) is constrained by strict conditions including Surah 2:190–194 (no transgression) and Surah 22:39 (only those attacked may fight). Reducing jihad to “holy war” is a misconception.
  • Id-ul-Adha commemorates Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son (Surah 37:77–111); Id-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. Both are shared Sunni–Shi’a festivals.
  • Id-ul-Ghadeer (Shi’a) commemorates Muhammad’s announcement of Ali as successor at Ghadir Khumm — anchored in Surah 5:3. Ashura has contrasting Sunni (fasting/gratitude) and Shi’a (mourning for Imam Husayn at Karbala) meanings.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Islamic beliefs about Jihad.
practice_questions.model_answer: Three from: Jihad means 'striving' or 'struggle' (not simply holy war); greater jihad is the inner struggle against the lower self (nafs); lesser jihad is outward defensive struggle permitted only under strict conditions; Surah 2:190-194 conditions lesser jihad (no transgression); Surah 22:39 permits defensive jihad for those who are attacked. One mark per clearly distinct point.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Muslims celebrate at Id-ul-Adha.
practice_questions.model_answer: Id-ul-Adha commemorates Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to Allah. It coincides with the end of the Hajj pilgrimage. Muslims sacrifice an animal (qurbani) and share the meat with family, friends and the poor. It involves communal prayer and is one of the two major Islamic festivals. Three descriptive points earn three marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between how Sunni and Shi'a Muslims observe Ashura.
practice_questions.model_answer: First difference: For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is primarily a day of voluntary fasting. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari records that the Prophet observed the fast and encouraged it as a day of gratitude commemorating Moses being saved from Pharaoh. It is an optional act of devotion with no element of mourning. Second difference: For Shi'a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year — a day of mourning and lamentation for the martyrdom of Imam Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Shi'a Muslims hold processions, re-enactments and lamentations. This reflects the Shi'a theological significance of Husayn's sacrifice as a defining moment in their religious identity. Two developed points, two marks each.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why greater jihad is considered important in Islam.
In your answer you must refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.model_answer: First reason: Greater jihad is central to personal spiritual development. Every act of worship — prayer, fasting, charity — requires overcoming the lower self (nafs). Without this inner struggle, outward religious practice can become hollow habit. The Qur'an commands believers to strive for God: Surah 22:39 describes the striving of those who have been wronged, but the broader context of the surah is that striving for God encompasses all dimensions of life. Second reason: Greater jihad is the most continuous form of jihad, lasting from birth to death. It cannot be completed and set aside. This makes it, in classical Islamic scholarship, the greater of the two forms. The named source — Surah 2:190-194 constrains lesser jihad with conditions, implying that the unconditioned inner struggle is the more fundamental obligation. The fifth mark requires a named surah reference.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the statement: 'The true meaning of jihad has been misunderstood by most people.'
In your answer you should give developed arguments in support of and against this statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.model_answer: Arguments in support: The word jihad in Arabic simply means 'striving' and covers all effort made in the way of Allah — including prayer, charity, care for family and personal self-improvement. Greater jihad (the inner struggle against nafs) is considered by classical scholars to be the more important form. Surah 2:190-194 places strict conditions on lesser jihad, making it a constrained, last-resort defence — not an open call to violence. Media and political discourse has reduced a rich theological concept to a single-dimensional caricature of violence. Many Muslims — scholars and practitioners alike — argue that this misrepresentation harms both the religion and wider social understanding. Arguments against: While the inner-struggle interpretation is important, it would also be wrong to suggest that lesser jihad (outward struggle) is not a genuine part of Islamic teaching. The Qur'an does address defensive warfare directly in Surah 2:190-194 and Surah 22:39. Some Islamic scholars throughout history have emphasised outward jihad in specific historical and political contexts. The statement risks overcorrecting — portraying jihad as purely spiritual and ignoring its legitimate outward dimensions. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might argue that most people have misunderstood jihad by reducing it exclusively to violence, since this ignores the greater jihad and the strict conditions on lesser jihad. However, the statement is slightly too absolute — jihad does include an outward dimension that is genuinely part of Islamic teaching, not an invention of misreaders. The fullest understanding acknowledges both dimensions in their proper relationship. Mastering (10-12): both sides developed with Qur'anic anchors (Surah 2:190-194, Surah 22:39); explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides; one source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant. Emerging (1-3): brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three facts about the Shi'a festival of Id-ul-Ghadeer.
practice_questions.model_answer: Three from: Id-ul-Ghadeer commemorates the event at Ghadir Khumm in 632 CE; the Prophet Muhammad announced Ali as his rightful successor (according to Shi'a belief); the anchor verse is Surah 5:3 ('Today I have perfected your religion'); it is specifically significant to Shi'a Muslims and relates to the doctrine of Imamah; Sunni Muslims interpret Surah 5:3 differently. One mark per clearly distinct point.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Shi'a significance of Ashura?

flashcard_questions.a: Voluntary fasting in gratitude, commemorating Moses being saved from Pharaoh.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the Sunni significance of Ashura?

glossary_terms.definition: An Arabic word meaning 'striving' or 'struggle' — the effort a Muslim makes to live according to Allah's will, in both personal and communal dimensions.
The continuous inner spiritual struggle to resist the lower self (nafs), overcome temptation and live as a good Muslim.
The outward struggle to defend the Muslim community or uphold justice, permitted only under strict conditions as a last resort.
The lower self or ego in Islamic teaching — the inner desires and impulses that can lead a person away from God's path.
The Festival of Sacrifice, commemorating Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to Allah, celebrated during the Hajj period.
The festival marking the end of Ramadan, celebrated with prayer, charity (Zakat al-Fitr), feasting and family visits.
A Shi'a festival commemorating the Prophet Muhammad's announcement of Ali ibn Abi Talib as his successor at Ghadir Khumm, anchored in Surah 5:3.
The tenth of Muharram. For Sunni Muslims: a voluntary fast commemorating Moses. For Shi'a Muslims: a day of mourning for the martyrdom of Imam Husayn at Karbala in 680 CE.
